title: What to Know About Shamonda Virus Following the First Reported Human Infection
gist: France has confirmed that a severely immunocompromised patient in Lyon died after the first known human infection with Shamonda virus, a midge-borne livestock virus first identified in Nigeria in the 1960s. Authorities call the case exceptional and say there is no risk to the general public. The virus is spreading in European livestock, though. A new Shamonda-Europe variant was detected in Switzerland this summer and later in at least eight more countries, including on farms in 37 French provinces.

insights.claim: France confirmed the death in Lyon of the first known human infected with Shamonda virus, a livestock virus previously considered non-transmissible to humans. The patient was severely immunosuppressed, and authorities say there is no risk to the general public.
insights.speaker: Fernanda González
insights.so_what: This is a new zoonotic spillover signal, but officials currently judge the public-health risk to be low.
insights.quote: The neurological complications observed in the immunocompromised patient prior to his death were most likely related to infection with the Shamonda virus
insights.locator: The report specifies that the case occurred in Lyon.

insights.claim: University of Glasgow virologist Ben Brennan says the patient's serious underlying illness means it is not yet known whether Shamonda virus contributed to the death.
insights.speaker: Ben Brennan
insights.so_what: The case does not yet establish a causal link between the virus and human deaths.
insights.quote: we do not yet know whether Shamonda virus contributed to their death

insights.claim: David Roiz of Spain's Institute for Game and Wildlife Research argues that globalized movement of animals and goods and a changing climate make sporadic human cases of animal viruses unsurprising. He says they call for monitoring, not alarm.
insights.speaker: David Roiz
entities: Institute for Game and Wildlife Research
insights.so_what: Climate change and trade are structural drivers of emerging vector-borne disease risk in Europe.
insights.quote: In a globalized world, where animals and goods are on the move and the climate is changing, it is not unusual for cases of human transmission to occur

insights.claim: A new Shamonda-Europe variant was detected in Swiss livestock this summer and later found in Germany, France, Austria, Belgium, the Netherlands, Liechtenstein, Italy and Spain. Until a few months ago, Europe was considered free of the virus.
insights.speaker: Fernanda González
insights.so_what: The rapid spread across the continent poses a risk to European cattle and dairy output.
insights.locator: Still, several European countries are on alert

insights.claim: Spain's Ministry of Agriculture, Fisheries and Food says two genetically distinct forms, Shamonda Type 1 and Type 2, are circulating in Europe. Infections of both types were confirmed on livestock farms in 37 French provinces in early September.
insights.speaker: Fernanda González
entities: Spain’s Ministry of Agriculture, Fisheries, and Food
insights.so_what: Widespread farm-level infection in France points to possible agricultural losses and trade restrictions.
insights.locator: Spain’s Ministry of Agriculture, Fisheries, and Food states

insights.claim: Shamonda virus spreads between animals mainly through biting midges and has a 2-3 day incubation period. It causes fever, diarrhea and lower milk production in cattle, and miscarriages or calf deformities in pregnant cows. No vaccine exists, so control relies on insecticides and repellents.
insights.speaker: Fernanda González
insights.so_what: Without a vaccine, demand for vector control rises and there is an opening for animal-health vaccine developers.
insights.quote: To date, there is no vaccine, so prevention and control measures rely on the use of insecticides and repellents.
insights.locator: After animal is bitten by a midge
